titre: The Home Insurance Building May Not Have Been the First Skyscraper
accroche: Chicago put up a plaque in 1932 for its 1885 “first skyscraper”: architectural historians are no longer so sure today.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1885, architect William Le Baron Jenney completes a ten-story building in Chicago for the Home Insurance Company: 42 meters (138 feet) tall, soon raised to 55 meters (180 feet) after two floors are added in 1891. Part of its structure, columns and beams, is made of steel and iron, and carries the facade instead of the facade carrying its own weight. In 1932, a plaque placed on the site calls Jenney the “true father of the skyscraper.” At the building's centennial, in 1985, the title of world's first skyscraper is attached to it without apparent reservation, and it has since found its way into most textbooks.

## A Title Older Than Its Evidence

The Home Insurance Building was nonetheless demolished in 1931, a year before its own commemorative plaque was installed, and forty years before architectural historians began to look more closely at the claim. It never had, on completion, a structure entirely carried by a metal frame: it mixes load-bearing masonry with iron elements, a solution already used elsewhere. The press of the time does not present it as a first either: an 1884 article lists three buildings under construction in Chicago meant to surpass it in height.

## Earlier Rivals

Metal frames exist before it: the Ditherington flax mill, in England, as early as 1797, five stories on a structure entirely of cast iron, and Philadelphia's Broad Street Station, in 1881, six stories on a steel frame. Neither is tall enough to claim the word skyscraper, but they show the technique was not born in Chicago in 1885. In 2019, the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat, the body that keeps height rankings worldwide, confirms to the Chicago Tribune that no recognized criterion settles what makes a first skyscraper, and that it does not rule out stripping the Home Insurance Building of the title.

## What Remains

The building still holds a real place: it is one of the first to use a metal frame to carry a facade across several floors, in a city then inventing tall construction through successive trial and error. But the point is not that it came first, it is that there is no clear finish line: the skyscraper was not born on a single day, it was assembled piece by piece, in several cities at once, before Chicago kept the name.

repere.texte: Load-bearing metal frames predate the Home Insurance Building (1885): England's Ditherington flax mill carries one entirely of cast iron as early as 1797, and Philadelphia's Broad Street Station one of steel as early as 1881.

carte.punch: The “world’s first skyscraper” may never have existed.
carte.idee: In 1885, Chicago's Home Insurance Building supposedly invented the skyscraper, a title engraved on a plaque as early as 1932. Its structure, however, mixed steel and masonry, and metal frames already existed elsewhere: no recognized criterion settles a winner.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Details the dispute over the first-skyscraper title and the rival buildings.

quiz.question: Why is the title of “world's first skyscraper,” given to Chicago's Home Insurance Building (1885), disputed by historians today?
choix: Because the building collapsed before it was finished, in 1884
Because its structure mixed steel and masonry, and metal frames already existed elsewhere
Because William Le Baron Jenney was not an architect but a bridge engineer
Because the Home Insurance Company went bankrupt before the building's opening
quiz.explication: Its structure mixed steel and load-bearing masonry, and metal frames already existed elsewhere before it; the building was never left unfinished, Jenney was indeed an architect, and the company did not go bankrupt before the opening.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which earlier metal structure, predating the Home Insurance Building (1885), is cited as a rival for the title of first load-bearing metal frame?
choix: The Ditherington flax mill (1797), in cast iron
quiz_supplementaire.explication: England's Ditherington flax mill uses a frame entirely of cast iron as early as 1797, nearly ninety years before the Home Insurance Building; the other three examples are later, or are not load-bearing building frames carrying a facade.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which organization confirmed in 2019 that no recognized criterion could settle a single “first skyscraper”?
choix: The Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat, which keeps the world ranking of tall buildings, confirmed this to the Chicago Tribune in 2019, without ruling out stripping the Home Insurance Building of the title.
